In this problem set we are going to replicate one of the main findings from Bertrand, Duflo and Mullainathan (2004).  We will do this in a series of steps that we will then put together into one big simulation at the end.

First things first, we will need the *tidyverse* and *plm* packages, so use this 
code chunk to install (if needed) and load them

```{r, echo=FALSE, results='hide', message=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
#these are the necessary packages 
packages = c("tidyverse","plm")

#this function checks if you have the necessary packages
#if you have them it loads them, if you don't it installs and loads them
package.check <- lapply(packages, FUN = function(x) {
  if (!require(x, character.only = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(x, dependencies = TRUE)
    library(x, character.only = TRUE)
  }
})
```

Now we need to load the 1979-1999 CPS data for women aged 25-50. I have downloaded 
and cleaned this in a separate file which you can download from Canvas (bertrand_04_collapsed.dta).  Alter this
code chunk to set your working directory to wherever you have saved the data and 
then load it. Alternatively, you can just make sure the dataset is in the same
file as this script and you do not need to change the working directory.

```{r, echo=TRUE}
#change this to a working directory where the data is saved
#setwd()
bertrand_data <- haven::read_dta("../data/bertrand_04_collapsed.dta")
```

Next, we are going to run simulations where we randomly select a *treatment year* 
and then randomly assign 25 states as treated.  We will then run the traditional 
DiD specification to see if there is a treatment *effect*.  Since there is no actual 
treatment, this should *almost always* result in a treatment effect where we *fail*
to reject the null hypothesis.

Before we run simulations, we need to create the code that will do all of the steps 
we just outlined.

First, we need to write some code that will randomly select a year between 1979-1999
as the treatment year.  There are a number of ways you can do this, but I suggest 
using either the *sample()* function or you can combine the *round()* and *runif()*
functions together.

Use this code chunk to write some code which will randomly pick a year between 1980-1999
(you don't want to include 1979 because that will mess up our regressions later)

You should store the year that is selected as an object called **intervention_year**,
then put that objects name at the end of the code chunk so that you can repeatedly 
run the chunk and have R spit out a new intervention_year, which should bounce around 
from 1980-1999.

```{r, echo=TRUE}
intervention_year = 
  sample(1980:1999, size = 1)
intervention_year
```


Next, we need to randomly select 25 of the 50 states in order to assign them as 
treated.  I have done the first piece for you, which is to make a list of the 50 
states from out dataset using the *unique()* command and storing it as a data frame
called 'state_list'.

```{r, echo=TRUE}
#create list of states to assign treatment to
state_list <- as.data.frame(unique(bertrand_data$state))
colnames(state_list) <- c("state")

# selected_states =
  # sample(state_list$state, size = 25)
```


Next, we need to randomly select 25 of the 50 states.  There are many ways you could 
do this, but I suggest the following four steps:

1 - Create a new variable called **random** which assigns a number between 0 and 1 to each state using the *runif()* command

2 - Sort the data based on this new variable using *arrange()*

3 - Create another new variable that is a count of the states as they are ordered using *row_number()*.  Call this variable **n**

4 - Create a treatment variable that is 1 for all observations with **n** less than
or equal to 25

Do this below. Since we are using tidyverse, you can combine all four steps using
the %>% piping

```{r, echo=TRUE}
state_list = state_list |> 
  mutate(random = runif(n(), min = 0, max = 1)) |> 
  arrange(random) |> 
  mutate(n = row_number(), 
         treatment = if_else(n <= 25, 1, 0))

state_list
```

Now we have our 25 randomly selected states.  Next, we need to merge this with our 
original dataset.  Do this using the *merge()* command, and call this new dataset
**bertrand_treat**. Merge the two datasets by the "state" variable

```{r, echo=TRUE}
bertrand_treat = 
  merge(bertrand_data, state_list, by = "state", all.x = TRUE)
```

Now, create a new variable called **year_treat** that is 1 if the year in the dataset 
is **greater than or equal** to **intervention_year**, which we created earlier, and 0 otherwise.

Finally, create a variable called **treated**, which is the product of **year_treat** and
**state_treat**.  This is our treatment variable we will use in our regression.

Create these two variables in the code chunk below

```{r, echo=TRUE}
bertrand_treat = bertrand_treat |> 
  mutate(year_treat = if_else(year >= intervention_year, 1, 0),
         treated = year_treat*treatment
         )

bertrand_treat
```

Ok, we have now set up our regression.  Since we have not covered DiD yet, I am 
going to provide the code to run our regression, and I am going to call it plm1.

```{r, echo=TRUE}
#run regression and view results
plm1 <- plm(uearnwk ~ treated, 
    data = bertrand_treat, index = c('state', 'year'), model = 'within',
    effect = 'twoways')
summary(plm1)
```

Let's also store the p-value from our regression.  If you run

```{r, echo = TRUE}
summary(plm1)$coefficients
```

It returns a matrix with the coefficients from the regression. We want to create an 
object called **p_value** which stores the p-value from this matrix.  

Do this below.  It is simple to do, but it may take some googling if you have not 
worked with matrices in R.

```{r, echo = TRUE}
p_value = summary(plm1)$coefficients[4]
p_value
```


Now that we have our code to run their specification, we just need to do this a 
whole bunch of times.

I am going to create an empty data frame which you will use to store the p-values
from 1,000 replications of what we have just done.

```{r, echo = TRUE}
df <- data.frame(matrix(ncol=2,nrow=1000))
```

Next, copy all of your code from each code chunk above after the brackets below, starting
with the chunk where you loaded the data and ending with the chunk that stores the p-value from the regression.  Make sure you do this in order. When you are done, you should be able to run the new (large) code chunk and it will run through our specification 1,000 times and store all of the p-values.

If you have done this correctly, it will take a little bit of time to run, but shouldn't
take more than a minute or two.

```{r}
bertrand_data <- haven::read_dta("../data/bertrand_04_collapsed.dta")

for (i in 1:1000) {
  
  intervention_year = 
    sample(1980:1999, size = 1)
  
  state_list <- as.data.frame(unique(bertrand_data$state))
  colnames(state_list) <- c("state")
  
  state_list = state_list |> 
    mutate(random = runif(n(), min = 0, max = 1)) |> 
    arrange(random) |> 
    mutate(n = row_number(), 
           treatment = if_else(n <= 25, 1, 0))
  
  bertrand_treat = 
    merge(bertrand_data, state_list, by = "state", all.x = TRUE)
  
  bertrand_treat = bertrand_treat |> 
    mutate(year_treat = if_else(year >= intervention_year, 1, 0),
           treated = year_treat*treatment)
  
  plm1 <- plm(uearnwk ~ treated, 
              data = bertrand_treat, index = c('state', 'year'), model = 'within',
              effect = 'twoways')
  
  p_value = summary(plm1)$coefficients[4]

  df[i,1] <- i
  df[i,2] <- p_value
}  
```

Lastly, write some code to see how often our regression rejected the null hypothesis
of no treatment effect at the 5% significance level.

```{r}
table(df[, 2] < 0.05)
# True is the number of null rejections
```

Is this more or less than you would expect?
